open_obligations: Check that the two framings in Sudhir et al. are both consistent with Bowman et al.'s definition.
Note that Sudhir et al.'s benchmark measures the training-signal framing via ASD.
Check whether inference-time oversight is evaluated at all in the benchmark.
in.other_title: Scalable oversight as a training method or as an inference-time oversight mechanism
in.rationale: Bowman et al. define scalable oversight as reliable supervision that remains effective past broadly human-level performance. Sudhir et al. cite Bowman et al. and describe it as a feedback mechanism that scales to superhuman intelligence, framing it either as a training method making honesty the best policy or as an inference-time mechanism-design problem, which motivates their ASD metric.
in.scope: proposed DEPENDS_ON: the definition of scalable oversight used to design a protocol benchmark

open_obligations: Note the shift from 'too expensive to evaluate' to 'beyond human-level'.
Check which of Amodei et al.'s approaches (semi-supervised RL, distant supervision) Bowman et al.'s definition still covers.
Check that experiments citing either definition test the same problem.
out.other_title: Scalable oversight: correct objective known but too expensive to evaluate often
out.rationale: Amodei et al. describe scalable oversight as the case where the correct objective is known or can be evaluated, e.g. by a human, but too expensively to do often. Bowman et al. define scalable oversight as providing reliable supervision (labels, rewards, critiques) that stays effective past human-level performance, citing Amodei et al.; the emphasis shifts from evaluation cost to capability beyond the supervisor.
out.scope: proposed DEPENDS_ON: the definition of scalable oversight used to frame empirical oversight research
